/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.headline: UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.excerpt: The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country. Prime minister Andy Burnham will announce the move on Thursday at Cop31, the UN climate summit, with the new role designed to advise the government on national security risks from the climate crisis before they spell catastrophe. Burnham will tell the key climate talks on Thursday morning: “We should all recognise the summer was not normal. The climate crisis is upon all of us now. We saw that with the wildfires that devastated lives and livelihoods everywhere.” This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, with back-to-back heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis causing health services and transport to suffer, schools to close and thousands of people to lose their lives prematurely. Burnham will add: “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future. The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down.
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.trail: Exclusive: Madeleine Alessandri, chair of the joint intelligence committee, will take on the role of advising No 10 on climate-related national security risks

/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.headline: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.excerpt: Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit. Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals. She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later. “It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.” Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement. “The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up. “Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.” The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.trail: Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms

/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.headline: National security of all countries at risk due to climate crisis, UK foreign secretary warns
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.excerpt: The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey. Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict. “National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news,” Miliband told the Guardian before his speech to world leaders and governments in Antalya. “We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face. Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis],” he said. In a veiled swipe at the Conservatives and Reform UK, which want to scrap efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, he added: “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.” Miliband arrived in Turkey on Tuesday evening for the two-day leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday and Thursday of the fortnight-long Cop31 talks, which started on Monday.
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.trail: Exclusive: Ed Miliband says sci-fi scenarios of destruction ‘now regular occurrences’, as he prepares to address Cop31

/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.headline: UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.excerpt: Turkey and Australia, the co-hosts of crucial climate talks, must urgently move from discussing the end of fossil fuels to delivering it, the UN chief has said. “It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” António Guterres said, in a dramatic intervention on the second day of the conference on Tuesday. “Now, here at Cop31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it.” The two countries hosting Cop31 are significant exporters of fossil fuels. Early on Tuesday, the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, was extolling his country’s oilfields even as he prepared for his appearance at the summit on Wednesday. Guterres said the talks should end with “clear next steps” to advance a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels presented to delegates on Tuesday by Brazil, which presided over last year’s talks. During a presentation with the Brazilians, Guterres – who will step down as UN secretary general at the end of this year and has made the climate crisis a central part of his agenda, often intervening on issues with dramatic language – was energetically backed by the former US secretary of state and climate envoy John Kerry, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, and his predecessor, the Mexican diplomat Patricia Espinosa. He was met by rapturous applause as he left the stage.
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.trail: António Guterres calls for ‘clear next steps’ as countries face pressure to agree concrete measures

/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.headline: Cop31 may involve lots of talking about talking – but there are wins to be had
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.excerpt: The world has again convened for Cop, the annual ritual to confront humanity’s greatest-ever threat. Aside from its own lore and acronyms, this conference is starting to feel a little like Groundhog Day. Representatives from almost all countries, bar the recalcitrant version of the US under Donald Trump, are here in Antalya, Turkey, to face a familiar if worsening challenge. (Even the Taliban are attending.) The UN, which oversees these talks, has acknowledged the obvious fact that the previously agreed 1.5C global temperature-rise limit is set to be breached in just a few years, with the Earth amassing heat at an accelerating pace. Wealthy countries, though, are still failing to meet commitments to assist poorer, vulnerable nations to cope with climate impacts. We are still cutting emissions far too slowly. We are still bickering over who should shoulder the most responsibility for this. So what’s to be gained from Cop31? We’ll go into what to expect over the next two weeks, after this week’s most important reads – and a reminder that, through Cop31, Down to Earth will be coming to you twice a week from Guardian reporters here in Antalya. Essential reads Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve? ‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate Alien menace or victim of xenophobia?
/environment/2026/nov/12/world-heading-f.trail: In this week’s newsletter: what to expect of the next two weeks. Plus, this week’s most important reads

/technology/2026/nov/12/facial-recogniti.headline: Police use facial recognition to scan one million faces in WA trial leading to 122 arrests
/technology/2026/nov/12/facial-recogniti.excerpt: More than a million people have had their faces scanned in a trial of real-time facial recognition technology in Western Australia, resulting in 122 arrests and nine incorrect alerts. WA police said under the five-month trial, which concluded on Saturday, the technology scanned 1,380,882 faces after 100 deployments across 43 regional and metropolitan locations. Alongside the 122 arrests, the alerts led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders and locate 10 people for a welfare check. The deployments included three operations at the Perth royal show, where 223,749 faces were scanned, resulting in 15 alerts, three arrests and seven “interactions” with registered sex offenders. A police spokesperson confirmed the system generated nine incorrect alerts against the total 1.38m scans, meaning there was an error rate of 0.00065%. Addressing the false matches at a media conference on Sunday, the WA police commissioner, Col Blanch, confirmed officers engaged with each individual. “I want to be very clear on those false alerts,” he said. “No one was arrested. No one made a complaint. Each one did result in an interaction with that person and asking them relevant questions. “It’s a very, very, very low number. It’s not zero. We’d love it to be zero.
/technology/2026/nov/12/facial-recogniti.trail: Deployments of surveillance vans over five months resulted in nine false alerts and led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders

/technology/2026/nov/12/facial-recogniti.headline: ‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims
/technology/2026/nov/12/facial-recogniti.excerpt: AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research. Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG). It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool. Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry. The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.
/technology/2026/nov/12/facial-recogniti.trail: Tasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights Group

/us-news/2026/nov/11/scott-colom-mississ.headline: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
/us-news/2026/nov/11/scott-colom-mississ.excerpt: Hundreds of people gathered across from the Mississippi state capitol building on Thursday evening to rally against the aggressive Republican efforts to draw maps that favor their own party. Shortly after the US supreme court’s decision in Louisiana v Callais, which severely weakened section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, Tate Reeves, the Mississippi governor, moved in lockstep with other Republican governors and lawmakers to call for a special session to redraw maps. However, before that special session could occur, Reeves canceled it and wrote on X that he expected “lawmakers to redraw congressional lines BETWEEN NOW and 2027 elections!” In August, members of the Mississippi legislature’s joint redistricting committee began a tour of eight redistricting hearings across the state. The last of those hearings took place Thursday evening in Jackson, the state’s capitol. “This fight is familiar territory for all of us. The giants of the civil rights movement didn’t fight so that we could sit this fight out. They fought so we could stand exactly where we’re standing right now and finish what they started,” Safia Malin, policy director at One Voice, a civic organization, told the crowd before the hearing.
/us-news/2026/nov/11/scott-colom-mississ.trail: Dozens of residents testify to legislature’s redistricting committee in heated hearing, the last of eight

/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.headline: Vetting candidates is a tricky process but Reform can’t seem to get it right
/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.excerpt: Speaking to reporters after unveiling his new defence spokesperson this week, Nigel Farage’s jovial and upbeat mood suddenly switched. Why, he was asked, was a Reform UK councillor who was arrested in January over multiple alleged sexual offences still in his role nearly 10 months later? “I have no idea,” Farage replied icily. “I was told yesterday, and I wasn’t very happy.” A later question about Reform’s misfiring processes for vetting candidates did nothing to improve the mood. Why, Farage asked, was wrongdoing in other parties barely covered, when the news that the arrested Reform councillor had been charged prompted a BBC News alert? In fairness to the BBC, the charges brought against George Madgwick, who was Reform’s leader on Hampshire county council, were many and deeply serious, 35 in all, including 12 allegations of rape. Madgwick has said he is innocent. But more generally, it is another difficult moment for a party that has had to expand and professionalise at unprecedented speed, a process that its internal structures have at times failed to keep up with. Little more than a week earlier, it emerged that a member of Farage’s security team, Ryan Dinnage, who was with him during this year’s local elections campaign, was facing a rape charge at the time for which he was later convicted and jailed. Reform UK said they were unaware of the charge and that Dinnage “ceased to be used” by the party when it came to light.
/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.trail: Charges against party members and off-piste remarks highlight problems brought about by rapid expansion

/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.headline: EHRC raises concern with Reform about ‘racial and sexual remarks’ in documentary
/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.excerpt: The official equalities watchdog has written to Reform UK to raise concerns after an undercover TV documentary showed councillors and candidates for the party expressing racist and misogynistic views, with one of the party’s MPs complaining about ingrained sexism. The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it had written to Nigel Farage’s party in the wake of revelations in ITV’s Undercover: A Year in Reform, which was broadcast in October. While Farage has said the party’s vetting procedures have improved greatly, footage in the programme included Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, making Islamophobic remarks, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues. In another section, the Reform MP Sarah Pochin was shown complaining that the party was “chauvinistic” and riven with “alpha male shit”. An EHRC statement said its letter had asked Reform to provide information, “including what action the party is taking to comply with the Equality Act”.
/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.trail: Watchdog writes to Nigel Farage’s party to ask what action it is taking to comply with the Equality Act

/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.headline: Nigel’s ‘chiselled cheekbones’ make the news – Reform’s the Reformer, digested by John Crace
/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.excerpt: THE REFORMER Welcome to your new super, soaraway Reformer. The paper that aims to take you back to the 1950s with all the stories that the mainstream media don’t want you to read. Free to all patriots. And those who happen to have found a copy on the floor of the bus. A message from the editor, Nigel Farage We are living in dangerous times. The chances of finding an immigrant ahead of you in the supermarket checkout queue have never been higher. Now more than ever you need a newspaper you can trust. One that isn’t afraid to tell you the truth about Broken Britain, and where you can find a grievance on every page. So let me introduce you to the Reformer team. There’s me, Nigel. I’m the editor-in-chief. And then there are seven or eight other nobodies whose names escape me. Here is my promise to you. If you are not fully satisfied with the Reformer in the first 100 days then I will sack all the people I have already forgotten. FARMING IN CRISIS by Nigel Farage, agriculture editor A sensational report that has been hushed up by establishment figures linked to the European Union reveals that migrants are responsible for the failure of this summer’s harvest. The report, which has been leaked to the Reformer by a source who wishes to go by the name of Nigel, reveals that officials have tried to blame the crop failure on climate change. “It’s a total scandal,” said Nigel.

/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.headline: Security guard who protected Nigel Farage on campaign trail was facing rape charge
/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.excerpt: One of Nigel Farage’s security team who accompanied him on the local election campaign trail this year was facing a rape charge and was later jailed for eight years, raising questions about a failure of vetting. Ryan Dinnage spent time protecting Farage in April and May, but in June was convicted of having raped a woman while she slept in a caravan at the Royal Windsor horse show. Dinnage was seen beside Farage on walkabouts on at least four occasions on Reform’s local election campaign trail this spring: in Llandudno, Conwy County; Waterlooville, Hampshire, Worthing, West Sussex, and Downham Market, Norfolk. He had been charged in 2025, three years after the crime took place at the equestrian event in 2022. Reform UK acknowledged Farage was provided with protection by Dinnage, and said his services had been supplied by a third-party contractor who had assured them he had been vetted. A spokesperson for the party said: “As soon as we found out, we were shocked and disgusted and he ceased to be used by Reform.” However, the episode raises questions about how a security operative facing a charge of serious sexual violence could have been put in a position of responsibility near a senior politician and members of the public. Reform UK did not answer further questions about whether the party was continuing its relationship with the third-party contractor, and whether any action was taken against them.
/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.trail: Ryan Dinnage – who accompanied Reform UK leader on walkabouts before local elections – was later jailed, raising questions about vetting failure

/politics/2026/nov/11/senior-reform-uk-o.excerpt: A female Liberal Democrat MP has accused Nigel Farage of shoving her aside at the state opening of parliament after which one of her male colleagues intervened. Caroline Voaden gave her account of the incident in May this year after Farage revealed on Wednesday that there had been a “physical altercation” in parliament which meant he had decided to avoid the budget. Voaden told the Guardian: “He was trying to get out of the chamber and instead of just asking if he could go past, he said: ‘Let me past’. I turned round and said: ‘No, you can wait your turn like everyone else’. He grabbed me by the arm or the shoulder, pushed me to one side and tried to push past me. One of my colleagues tried to stop him because he thought I was going to fall down the stairs. And then we all shuffled down. “Quite deliberately, he grabbed me by the arm from behind and pushed me to one side so that I fell into a colleague or the wall on the other side. I was really taken aback and really angry because I think you just don’t behave like that in any workplace, let alone the chamber of the House of Commons. It was rude. It was nasty.” Voaden said she had complained to the serjeant at arms who she believed had written to Farage asking him to apologise. She also raised it with the speaker. “Nothing ever came of it,” she said. A Reform UK source said it was “not true at all, it was the Lib Dem MPs being aggressive towards Nigel.

/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.headline: Parents sue to stop Washington state trans sports ban that could require ‘invasive’ genital exams
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.excerpt: Parents of student athletes in Washington state have sued to block a ballot initiative banning transgender girls from women’s sports teams, calling the measure discriminatory and warning it would lead to “invasive” genital examinations for female athletes. Last week, voters in the solidly Democratic state passed Initiative 638, a major setback for LGBTQ+ rights amid the “blue wave” of the US midterm elections. Nebraska, Colorado and Arizona adopted similar anti-trans sports bans, though advocates say Washington state’s policy is particularly extreme due to its medical sex verification requirement for all girls who want to play team sports. The lawsuit was filed in state court on Monday by parents of trans and cisgender girls; TransFamilies, a non-profit Washington advocacy group; and the Washington Education Association, the teachers’ union. They are represented by the American Civil Liberties Union of Washington; Legal Voice, a group that fights gender discrimination; and Pacifica Law Group, a local firm. Washington’s measure mandates that girls provide documentation from medical providers about their sex before they join women’s teams, either through hormone or genetic tests or examinations of their “reproductive anatomy”. The policy does not apply to boys.
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.trail: Voters adopted extreme policy requiring medical sex verification for all girls who want to play team sports

/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.headline: The political playbook that unraveled US transgender rights in the past decade
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.excerpt: Shelby Chestnut remembers turning on the news in 2016 and hearing something he didn’t expect. Then- attorney general, Loretta Lynch, had just announced a federal lawsuit to block HB2 in North Carolina, otherwise known as the “bathroom bill”. Lynch said the law, which made it illegal for transgender people to use a public restroom that did not align with the sex listed on their birth certificate, was reminiscent of those passed during the Jim Crow era that restricted public facility use by race. Then, she addressed transgender Americans directly: “But no matter how isolated or scared you may feel today, the Department of Justice and the entire Obama administration wants you to know that we see you; we stand with you; and we will do everything we can to protect you going forward.” HB 2 was repealed within the year. Chestnut said he thought at the time: “Oh this is the next phase of protections for trans people.” But instead of the beginning of legal protections for transgender Americans – the past decade has become the exact inverse. This was made abundantly clear during the midterm elections, where even during a “blue wave” of tsunami proportions, ballot initiatives targeting transgender people were passed even in Democratic strongholds like Washington and Colorado. Just how much have things shifted?
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.trail: From the military to healthcare, Trump systematically dismantled Obama-era protections for transgender rights

/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.headline: ‘The blue wave isn’t applicable to trans people’: advocates in Washington state prepare to fight ban
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.excerpt: A coalition of advocacy groups are preparing to mount a legal challenge against a Washington state ballot initiative that bans transgender girls’ participation in girls’ school sports, which voters approved in last week’s midterm election and will go into effect next month. The challenge is poised to set off a protracted legal battle over the rights of trans youth in Washington, which has functioned as a safe haven for thousands of trans people fleeing states that have enacted anti-trans laws in recent years. If enforced, the ballot measure, Initiative 638, would be “the most extreme” trans sports ban of its kind, according to its opponents. The initiative’s official text says it would require all girls participating in school sports to “verify biological sex”, which could include confirming their “reproductive anatomy”. Opponents say that language potentially subjects tens of thousands of girls to invasive genital exams in order to participate in girls’ school sports. “There are parents that are going to be asking, ‘Is my kid going to have to have a choice of dropping their pants in front of a complete stranger or missing the track season?’ We don’t know the answer right now,” said Lexi Koren, a spokesperson for No Hate in Washington State, the campaign against I-638. Advocates say the state’s courts represent the likeliest path forward for any litigation, given relevant legal precedent, as well as strong state-level privacy and anti-discrimination statutes.
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.trail: Legal challenge against ballot initiative that bans transgender girls’ participation in girls’ school sports is poised to set off a battle over rights

/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.headline: ‘Sick to my stomach’: trans Americans on politicians who spent $183m attacking them for votes
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.excerpt: Metal Hennessy, a 19-year-old trans man who lives in Kansas, quoted one of his state’s most enduring exports – The Wizard of Oz – when describing the defeat of Roger Marshall, the incumbent Republican senator, on Tuesday: “Ding dong, the witch is dead.” This US midterm season, Kansans like Hennessy were subjected to a wave of anti-trans attacks as Marshall attempted to fight off a challenge from Democratic and Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton. The AP reported that Republicans pumped $7m into related ads, which aired 7,000 times in the state. Hennessy was not surprised that Republicans would target his community to win votes – earlier this year, a law took effect invalidating the driver’s licenses of trans people in the state and requiring them to use bathrooms in government buildings associated with their sex assigned at birth. Nor was Hennessy surprised the strategy failed. “I don’t think trans issues are a swing issue to the average cis-het population. Most people are concerned about gas prices or the economy,” he said. In the weeks leading up to Tuesday, Republicans spent an estimated $183m on ads about transgender issues. Elon Musk poured millions into political groups that attacked trans rights, intensely targeting Democrat James Talarico’s Senate run in Texas. Donald Trump, who successfully leveraged the culture war issue in 2024, stumped on it again, calling gender affirming care “mutilization” (meaning “mutilation”).
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.trail: Republicans spent big on midterms ads about transgender issues – and some Democratic candidates parroted anti-trans messaging, too

/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.headline: Washington state passes ballot measure banning trans girls from school sports
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.excerpt: Voters in Washington state have passed a ballot measure banning transgender girls from playing on girls’ sports teams, a major loss for LGBTQ+ rights in a solidly Democratic state. The measure says students in elementary, middle and high school who want to join girls’ athletics must first submit statements from their healthcare providers verifying their “biological sex”. Opponents have raised alarms the measure may force girls to endure “invasive and extreme” genital exams to participate in school sports. Initiative 638 passed with support from nearly 57% of voters as of Thursday morning, though votes were still being counted. More than 25 states across the US have adopted similar bans on trans youth athletes, mostly through legislation pushed by Republican lawmakers. Voters in Arizona and Nebraska approved similar ballot measures this week, and a ban proposed in Colorado was leading in early results, but that race has not yet been called. Prohibiting trans youth from sports has become a major priority of conservatives and anti-LGBTQ+ groups who argue that they are protecting “fairness” in women’s athletics. But civil rights advocates say the policies are discriminatory and unnecessary, noting that trans youth have long played sports and that the restrictions target a small group of students already facing extreme prejudice and exclusion.
/world/2026/nov/11/bridget-phillipson-ke.trail: Measure in blue state requires female athletes prove their sex, which critics warn could lead to ‘invasive’ genital exams

/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.headline: K-pop group NewJeans’s contract omitted rights to ‘sleep and free choice’ – report
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.excerpt: The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”. A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17. The contracts banned the performers from having an “insincere attitude” and engaging in “inappropriate romantic relationships”. They also struck standard child protection language which protected “basic human rights” including the group members’ right to education. The contracts from record label Ador (a subsidiary of Hybe, home of the popular groups BTS and Katseye) additionally excluded portions of the Korean government’s K-pop contract template stipulating that the label “shall not demand that a performer who is a minor engage in excessive physical exposure or overly sexually suggestive expression”. In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe representatives said the company adheres to child-protection laws and works hard to make sure its artists work and train in safe conditions. NewJeans are one of the decade’s most popular K-pop acts. In 2023, the five-member group followed Blackpink to become the second Korean girl-group to score a number one album on the Billboard charts. In November 2024, the band made global headlines when they announced their decision to leave the label amid contract disputes and claims that Ador had deliberately undermined their careers.
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.trail: New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors

/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.headline: Why is North Korea fortifying its border with South Korea?
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.excerpt: Last week North Korea hit the headlines with a vow to fire up its loudspeaker systems to blare propaganda into the South, but the latest dispute comes against a backdrop of militarisation of the border by Kim Jong-un that has been years in the making. Since April 2024, North Korea has been working on building a permanent fortified border through the demilitarised zone (DMZ) that divides the two sides, work that has led to a mine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers and plunged ties to new lows. Here’s a brief guide to what is being built, what Pyongyang says it’s for, and why even deciding where the border is has become such a fraught issue. What is North Korea building at the border? The 250km border is already fortified but not in the way many might traditionally think. It is more of a buffer than a barrier at the moment, in the form of a 4km-wide demilitarised zone (DMZ) which runs across the Korean peninsula. Since 2024, the North is thought to have laid about 960,000 mines in the DMZ, close to half of all the mines thought to be in an area that is already one of the most heavily mined places on earth. North Korea has also been constructing a continuous physical barrier on its side of the zone, along the full length of the line. It is made up of wire fencing, alongside minefields, tactical roads, and anti-tank barriers laid on ground stripped of vegetation.
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.trail: A row over a landmine blast and a threat to resume loudspeaker broadcasts has highlighted Kim Jong-un’s military ambitions

/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.headline: Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.excerpt: Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game. The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion. One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher. A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster. “We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed. They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.trail: Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street

/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.headline: Kim Jong-un crosses newly opened bridge into China
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.excerpt: Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour. The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency. He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship. Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua. Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said. The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950. Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted. Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.trail: North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member

/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.headline: Adoptees from Korea say they were abused and isolated in the US. Were they also ‘stolen’ from their birth parents?
/world/ng-interactive/2026/nov/12/how-na.excerpt: As international, transracial adoptees in their 30s in the US, Jacquelyn Wells and Lauren White-Gydas have things in common. They were both born in South Korea to unwed mothers in the 1980s. Both were shipped to the US as newborns to join white families who eagerly welcomed adorable, new daughters. And neither knew many other Asians in the towns where they grew up – Wells in Westford, Massachusetts, and White-Gydas in Salem, Oregon. But from there, their paths in the US split in dramatic, unpredictable ways. On a sunny spring day last year, Wells, 39, sat in her cozy home in southern Maine, her babbling, infant son nestled in her lap and wedding photos of her recent marriage to her first-generation Asian American spouse lining the walls. In one, Wells poses in her white gown alongside her beloved adoptive mom, who wears a gold dress, and her Korean birth mother, in a flowing hanbok. They beam, smiles emblematic of more than just the happy occasion. Wells was reunited with her biological parents, now married, and two full blood brothers during a trip to Seoul in 2018, when she was 31. She met her birth mother first, after reaching out through her adoption agency. “I was so afraid you were going to be so angry with me,” said her birth mother, who voluntarily relinquished Wells during a temporary breakup with Wells’s birth father. Wells, a singer-songwriter, had a concert booked in the city the next day. Right before she went on stage she got a text: “I’m your brother.

/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.headline: Poundland’s US owner says retailer remains ‘vulnerable’, after talks with ministers
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.excerpt: The US owner of Poundland has said the high street chain remains “challenged and vulnerable” after holding talks with ministers amid government criticism of its handling of the retailer. Gordon Brothers said on Thursday morning that it was still in “active discussions” with interested suitors and had been seeking to “protect as many jobs as possible”. Poundland filed a notice to appoint administrators last week, with the fate of its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers uncertain. Gordon Brothers, the US restructuring specialist that bought Poundland last year for £1 and launched a sale process for the company at the start of September, is under pressure to accept a bid to save the retailer, which is on the brink of collapse despite receiving solvent takeover offers. Last week the chain filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which gave the business 10 working days of breathing space from creditors to secure a potential rescue deal before potentially entering insolvency. The board of Poundland has lined up the advisory company AlixPartners to run the process after Gordon Brothers ceased providing funding. On Wednesday, executives from Gordon Brothers and Poundland separately held meetings with government ministers regarding the future of the retailer. Advisers are still in talks with parties interested in buying the brand and a large number of stores, about two months after a sale process was launched.
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.trail: Gordon Brothers still in ‘active discussions’ with interested parties and seeking to ‘protect as many jobs as possible’

/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.headline: Poundland staff could be out of work for years if retailer collapses, founder says
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.excerpt: The founder of Poundland has warned that staff at the retailer could be out of work for “years” if it collapses, as he called on the owners of the troubled chain to accept a proposed buyout deal. Steve Smith, who set up the firm with a store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, said: “Once these jobs are lost, they are lost” from Britain’s struggling high streets. His warning comes as the chain’s 12,000 employees face uncertainty over their future in the run-up to Christmas. Poundland’s future hangs in the balance after the retailer, which is controlled by the US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until 12 November while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the likelihood of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers have held back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade. Poundland’s management is scheduled to meet Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, on Wednesday as political pressure mounts on Gordon Brothers to accept an offer from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group rather than calling in administrators to break up the retailer. The restructuring firm is understood to believe that it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer.
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.trail: Steve Smith calls on owners to accept proposed buyout as 12,000 staff face uncertain future in run-up to Christmas

/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.headline: Poundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposed
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.excerpt: ‘It was a very successful and simple proposition,” laments one former Poundland boss. With every product in the shop sold at £1, and the price in its name, its proposition to shoppers was the clearest of any UK high street chain. Now the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer could disappear amid heavy competition and inflation that has eaten into its ability to offer bargains. Its potential collapse has brought distress for its up to 12,000 staff in the run-up to Christmas, and as shoppers head to the chain for Halloween costumes and treats. Meanwhile, its low-profile owners are facing questions from the prime minister over their behaviour in the week his government’s budget attempted to offer support to the high street. Poundland’s future hangs in the balance – and not for the first time – after the 36-year-old retailer filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland, from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the prospect of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers hold back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade.
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.trail: With the chain on the brink of administration, its low-profile US owners face questions about their conduct

/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.headline: Union in plea to save Poundland from administration, with 12,000 jobs at risk
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.excerpt: The shop workers’ union Usdaw has urged Poundland’s owners to reconsider a decision to prepare the budget chain for administration, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk. Gordon Brothers filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. Gordon Brothers previously rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland. It bought the struggling chain for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025. Only one bidder, Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family-owned company, was interested in buying the entire chain and working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, the chief executive. Gordon Brothers is understood to believe that it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer, which was worth less than the £30m in debts that Gordon Brothers took on when it bought the chain. The threat of administration leaves thousands of shop workers facing uncertainty in the run-up to Christmas. Rival cut-price retailers, including Poundstretcher, The Range and B&M, have reportedly expressed an interest in taking on some Poundland stores.
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.trail: Gordon Brothers files notice of intent to begin process after rejecting management-backed rescue bid

/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.headline: Poundland management in talks to lead bid that could save 11,000 jobs
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.excerpt: Poundland’s management team are in “advanced talks” to lead a bid for the ailing cut-price retailer that could save up to 11,000 jobs. The former Asda boss Andy Bond, who ran Poundland for a number of years from 2016 then stepped up to its former parent Pepco before leaving in 2025, is understood to be part of the negotiations to take on the business. The management buyout team, which includes the current boss, Barry Williams, is understood to be negotiating with an unnamed financial backer. Poundland’s current owners, Gordon Brothers, last month hired the advisory company Alvarez & Marsal to oversee a sale of the business at a reported price of £30m. The process has fuelled fears that the restructuring specialist is set on breaking up the retailer despite improved trading. Interested parties are thought to include the US company Fortress, which owns Poundstretcher, and Modella Capital, the UK-based private equity owner of Hobbycraft and TG Jones that this year put the UK arm of Claire’s and The Original Factory Shop into administration. Neither of these players are involved with Bond’s team. Sources said these financial companies were among those placing a first round of bids at the start of this week that are to be considered as early as Wednesday. One source said very few bids were expected to include the entire business and it was a “great shame” if an offer to keep the business trading was not considered.
/business/2026/nov/11/poundland-owner-ch.trail: Ex-Asda boss Andy Bond linked to plan, with buyout team understood to be negotiating with financial backer

/uk-news/2026/nov/12/bronze-leg-scottish.headline: What did the Romans ever give Scotland? Heated floors, flashy sandals, sun gods – and a lot of nails
/uk-news/2026/nov/12/bronze-leg-scottish.excerpt: Inveresk is a handsome village near Edinburgh that sits above a curve of the little river Esk, not far from the mighty Firth of Forth. It is full of elegant 18th-century houses and an attractive kirk, dated 1805. To the casual observer, there is absolutely nothing Roman about it. And yet, in 2010, when the local cricket pavilion was being rebuilt, an extraordinary find was made – two altars made of local sandstone, lying on their sides, evidently deliberately buried in the Roman era, dedicated to the gods Mithras and Sol. They had been made in the 140s CE as part of a mithraeum, a temple devoted to the worship of Mithras, a cult dependent on secret ritual and complex initiation ceremonies, much beloved by the Roman military. Carved from sandstone quarried nearby, the altars were impressive in scale and finely made, although terribly fragile. One of them had a frieze of four beautiful female faces carved into it: personifications of the four seasons. Spring was youthful and round-cheeked, winter was cloaked against the frost. Beneath the faces, a Roman mason had also carved the face of the sun god Sol, his rays hollowed right through the stone so that when a lamp was placed behind it, atmospheric flickers of light and shadow would have been thrown into the dark of the temple. There is also an iron hook behind the god’s mouth – archaeologist Fraser Hunter thinks for something metallic to hang there, to be set in motion and jangled by the convection of the lamp’s flame.
/uk-news/2026/nov/12/bronze-leg-scottish.trail: From steamy bathhouses to altars to Sol the sun god and leather shoes that still survive to this day, an eye-opening new exhibition chronicles Scotland under the Romans (before they fled)
